passage: In Istanbul, Omar had missed Selin's first gallery opening. He'd said he'd come straight from work; instead he stayed for a colleague's farewell and forgot to check the time. The next evening he knocked on her door without flowers. "Selin, I forgot your opening. That's the whole of it. I'm not going to blame work. I'm sorry." Selin crossed her arms. "It was my first show." "I know. I should have been there. What would help now?" She thought. "Come and see it properly. With me explaining every piece." "Saturday?" "Saturday." He took out his phone and, in front of her, put every one of her upcoming dates into his calendar with two reminders each. On Saturday he stayed at the gallery for two hours and asked about every painting. When they left, Selin took his arm.

qa.a: A colleague's farewell.

qa.q: Why did Omar come without flowers and without excuses?
qa.a: He felt genuinely sorry and wanted Selin to feel a real repair, not a gift or a story that pushed the blame onto work.

passage:
Santosh,

At Priya's wedding on Saturday, I imitated your accent in front of the whole table to get a laugh. You laughed too, but I saw your face afterwards. It was a cheap joke, and it hurt you. I'm sorry. I don't have an excuse. It wasn't the drinks or the crowd. It was me being careless with a friend.

I'd like to know what would help. If you'd like to talk, I'll come to you. If you'd rather I said something to the others at the table, I'll do that too.

And I've decided something for myself: I'm done with accent jokes. Not just about you. About anyone.

Tell me what you need.

Raghav

New family rule: home by six. SIX. Devika's birthday party is at five and goes till eight. So basically I can't go.

She asked if I wanted dal or sabzi. "Whatever."

She asked how school was. "Fine."

I did everything she asked. She can't say I didn't. But I'm SO angry I could scream. I'm just not going to give her the satisfaction.

subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]
passage: My name's Parveen. At school, I was the loud one. Class monitor, first to crack a joke, always arguing with the history teacher for fun. My friend Sumit said I was the bravest person he knew. At home, I was a different person. My uncle, who we lived with, was strict, and in his house I barely spoke. passage: Wasim, you asked how I got through end-sems last year. Okay, here's Rashmi's version. My grandmother died on the second day of exams. Nani, who basically raised me. My mother called at seven in the morning and I had a paper at ten. I remember thinking, very clearly: I'm going to put this in a box. Not now. And I did. I went to the exam. I studied every night. I didn't cry once. I got my best marks ever. But here's the thing I want you to hear. The day after the last paper, I took the train home, sat in Nani's room, and opened the box. I cried for two days straight. My mother held me. If I'd never opened it, I think I'd still be carrying it. The box helped. The opening mattered more.

passage:
Monday: Jatin's uncle, his mother's brother, died suddenly. Jatin's first end-semester exam was on Wednesday. He called home, then shut his laptop and opened his notes. "Later," he told himself. "I'll feel it later."
Exam week: Jatin studied every night, ate in the mess, and answered every paper. His roommate asked if he was okay. "Fine. After exams." He didn't cry once. He did well.
The Saturday after: Jatin took the bus home to Aligarh. His cousin Lalit, the uncle's son, met him at the gate. They didn't say anything. They sat on the steps where the uncle used to read the paper. Then Jatin started crying, and couldn't stop. Lalit cried too. They stayed there till evening. It was the first time Jatin had let himself feel it, and it felt like breathing out after holding it for a week.

qa.q: When was Jatin's first exam?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: Why did Jatin tell himself "I'll feel it later"?
qa.a: He felt the grief was too big to face with exams two days away, so putting the sorrow aside let him study.

qa.q: What made Jatin's pause healthy rather than harmful?
qa.a: He actually made time after exams to go home and grieve with his cousin, opening the box he'd shut.

qa.q: How might his cousin Lalit have felt when Jatin came home?
qa.a: Lalit probably felt deep sadness and some comfort at having someone to grieve with on his father's steps.

grounding: Shows a student boxing up grief to get through exams and then making time afterwards to grieve with family.

passage: Swati, you're worried because you haven't cried about your grandfather yet, with your exams on? Let me, Urmila Masi, tell you about my final year. My father died in March, a week before my final exams in Nagpur. My mother said, "Your father wanted you to finish." So I made a decision. I put him in a little box inside me. I wrote the exams. I didn't cry, not once. People thought I was hard-hearted. I did very well. But the most important choice I made wasn't the box. It was what I did after. The day after my last paper, I went to the river where he used to take me, alone, and I opened the box. I cried till sunset. And then I kept opening it, bit by bit, over the next year. That's what saved me. Not the closing. The opening.

qa.q: When did Urmila's father die?
qa.a: In March, a week before the final exams.

qa.q: Why did young Urmila decide to put the grief in a box?
qa.a: She felt her father would want her to finish, and setting the sadness aside let her get through the exams.

qa.q: What was the most important choice in the story, and why?
qa.a: Going to the river after the last paper to open the box and grieve, and continuing to do so over the next year, which let her heal.

qa.q: How might the people who thought her hard-hearted have been wrong?
qa.a: They saw only the closed box and didn't know Urmila was holding deep grief until there was time to feel it.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a student setting grief aside during exams and then opening it afterwards to grieve.

passage:
Hemant,

I'm writing this because when I try to say it at night, we're both too tired.

Yesterday I heard you on the phone with that difficult supplier. You were so patient. You listened to him for forty minutes, you made a joke, you calmed him right down. I remember falling in love with that voice.

Then you came to bed and I asked how your day was, and you said, "Don't start." I know you didn't mean anything. I know you're exhausted.

But I've noticed it's like this most days. You give all your kindness out there, and by the time you get home, there's none left for us.

I'm not angry. I miss you. Could we try something, maybe a short walk before your last calls, or one evening a week with phones off?

Irawati

passage: In her Mumbai office, Nikita was known as unflappable.
